1:
Keil and Delitzsch divide the chapter in three: parable, interpretation applied to Zedekiah, and closing promise. Clarke can hardly praise it enough — images, composition and transitions making it one of the most perfect pieces of its size conceivable, the sudden turn from horror to glory dispelling every cloud so that a traveller looking for shelter goes on rejoicing. Calvin states the burden soberly: the Jews were fools to think themselves safe with God for an adversary. Gill sets the occasion, a people charged with breaking faith with God now charged with breaking faith with men.

Why the message comes as a riddle is asked by all. Henry denies any intent to baffle, since the meaning is given at once; the form is chosen so hearers will notice, feel, remember and repeat it, which is why similitudes were common with the prophets and parables with Christ. Calvin says the noun and verb answer each other, so that one might render it enigmatize an enigma, and distinguishes two uses of obscurity: sometimes God speaks so as not to be understood by the impious, here to wake a hardened people. Gill hears a whetting in the Hebrew, and Clarke a root meaning to pierce — not what pierces the mind but what the mind must pierce.

The first bird is identified without dispute. Clarke reads the figure clause by clause: great wings for an extensive empire, length of wing for speed of conquest, thick plumage for many subjects, varied colours for many nations. Ellicott notes the definite article in the original and derives the variegation from an empire of differing languages and customs. Calvin argues from greater to less: a man who took the kingdom easily while it was whole would make nothing of its ruins.

Over the mountain named they divide. Ellicott takes it for Jerusalem, since the cedar belongs there and the palace was named for its forest of cedar. Calvin thinks such interpreters labour in vain: the passage usually cited speaks of the temple, built of a great mass of cedar, whereas here the land is meant, the mountain named for its trees and because the allegory needed it.

The cropped shoot is Jeconiah, eighteen at his accession and taken within three months, Gill notes, no more able to resist than a twig against such a bird; he and Wesley read the young twigs as the princes generally. On the place he was carried to, Ellicott points out that the Hebrew says a land of Canaan, the word being used elsewhere for merchandise, and that the parallel clause settles the sense; the city had already been so called for its trade.

The willow is the substitute king. Gill stresses that the choice fell not on a stranger but on one of the blood royal, the captive king's uncle, renamed at his patron's pleasure; Clarke has him set by great waters because propped by a city on great rivers, as a willow depends on wet ground. Ellicott insists the arrangement was meant to work — not a satrap but a native prince, a kingdom low but flourishing, dependent and useful against Egypt, which is why its frustration provoked such rage. Calvin agrees the terms were tolerable, name and dignity and wealth all left.

The second bird is the Egyptian king Gill identifies with the ruler a Greek historian calls Apries, and to whom Ellicott gives no variegated feathers, since he ruled no such medley of peoples. Calvin finds an Egyptian irrigation custom behind the roots bending toward him, and thinks the ingratitude worse in a private man raised beyond expectation who would have been defended in trouble. Ellicott renders the closing threat to say that not even great power will raise the plant from its roots again; Wesley adds that no great force is needed, a kingdom uprooted as we uproot a tree that cumbers the ground.
11:
Ellicott is unsure whether the explanation followed at once or after an interval, and thinks the interval likelier: a spell of genuine puzzlement would leave the hearers more attentive when the answer came. Calvin says the same about purpose from the other side — plain speech would have been shrugged off by people practised in despising rebukes, while a riddle held them in suspense and prepared them. He also takes the occasion to repeat that the earlier identification of the mountain with the city is false, since while the speech was figurative its parts had to answer one another as tree answers branch.

The terms of the arrangement are set out plainly. Gill names the substitute king as the deported king's uncle and lingers on the throne-name given him, which means the justice of the Lord and was itself a standing reminder to keep the covenant or expect vengeance. Base, in Gill's reading, means a viceroy paying tribute and subjects paying tax, which is what the low vine stood for; Clarke adds that the state was to have no political weight and would sink at last into a client governorship. Calvin insists nothing was concealed: the conditions were published openly, so no plea of being outwitted was available, and they were moderate terms where hard ones could have been imposed.

Breaking them is treated as the crime of the chapter. Henry makes the argument general — ingratitude to a benefactor is a sin against God, every solemn oath calls God to witness, truth is a debt owed to all men, and treachery is worse, not better, when the true religion deals falsely with the false. Ellicott supplies the precedent that makes the point stick: an oath extracted by fraud from an earlier generation still bound the nation centuries later, and its violation was punished; and this king had been warned more than once through Jeremiah. Since the intrigues were current, exposing them mattered for the exiles who still counted the city safe. Wesley reduces it to a question about whether perjury can be a road to deliverance. Clarke narrows the date of the embassy to the months between two of the prophet's dated visions.

The reply is itself an oath, which Gill notes the Jewish commentators mark as such, sworn in anger by the divine life. Calvin uses it to argue restraint: God never brings his own name forward in vain, and by that example teaches us not to rush into swearing. He then faces a difficulty in the wording, since the man was to die in Babylon yet never saw it, his eyes having been put out at Riblah, and answers that the sentence means simply death in exile; Clarke states the same facts without treating them as a problem. Ellicott finds the form of the sentence exactly fitted to the crime — death in the city of the king who gave him his crown and received his fealty — and notes the tense turning future, since none of it had yet happened.

What Egypt would do is the last question. Ellicott corrects the rendering that makes the siege-works Pharaoh's own, since ramps and forts belong to a besieging and not a relieving army, and would read it of the time when they are cast up; he identifies the king as Hophra, records that an Egyptian force did come and lift the siege briefly, and that the Chaldeans drove it off, returned, and took and burned the city. Calvin rejects a rival reading on which the reproach is that Pharaoh promised fifty thousand and sent ten, as kings do when they make treaties; the point, he holds, is not that the help was undersized but that it was useless, since whatever was attempted would fail.
18:
The despised oath is stated a second time, which Gill takes as deliberate emphasis on the enormity and on the cause of the ruin. Clarke says the offence is particularly resented: the man had sworn in the divine presence to keep faith with his overlord and broke it at the first opportunity, so he will not escape. Calvin adds a piece of custom, reading the given hand as the gesture by which men witnessed an agreement, so that the alliance with Egypt is named here by the action that sealed it — a hand stretched out to one party while already pledged to another. Wesley notes only that the gesture solemnly confirms the oath.

Whose oath it was turns out to matter. Ellicott points out that the sworn covenant with a foreign king is called the Lord's, both because it was made in his name and because he had required it, from which it follows that rebelling against that king was, in these circumstances, apostasy from God himself. Calvin lays weight on the same possessive, and reads the whole sentence as confirmation of what preceded.

Why the confirmation needs an oath at all Calvin explains by the weakness of common conviction. Everyone holds, in some fashion, that treaties are sacred and that perjury is punished; but such notions are born with us and follow nature rather than faith, and they evaporate, because those who hold them do not hold the point on which they depend, that God judges the world. So the general persuasion has to be replaced by a specific declaration, with God himself named as the avenger, or the threat would not be believed.

The net is a figure Gill and Clarke both pass over quickly, referring back to the same image used earlier of the same man. Calvin makes more of it. The metaphor identifies the kind of punishment as capture rather than any other stroke, and it explains something recurrent in Scripture: an invading army acting on its own designs, taking one course and then another, is nonetheless the instrument of a God who governs it by a secret power and directs it where he pleases. Men throw everything into confusion and are driven about by their appetites, and still their attacks are moderated by a providence they know nothing of; that is what is meant by calling the enemy force a net belonging to God.

The scattering of the army closes the interpretation. Gill and Clarke agree that those who broke out when the city fell, and those who ran toward Egypt, were cut down; Calvin explains the mechanism, that troops in formation absorb and return an attack while troops dispersed are each at the enemy's mercy, so that a large force consulting its own safety piecemeal becomes a general slaughter, like refuse blown about by the wind. Wesley enters the usual caution that all here means the greater part rather than every man. Ellicott marks the boundary at this point: the explanation of the parable is finished, and what follows, though it keeps the same imagery, answers to nothing in either the parable or its interpretation.
22:
The promise answers an unstated objection. Gill puts it as the fear that the tribe was lost, the royal family extinct and the pledge of a perpetual throne void. Henry answers that the pledge was conditional, forfeited by a posterity that broke its terms, yet not cancelled: human unbelief does not invalidate a divine promise, and another seed will be found in which it holds. Keil and Delitzsch say it briefly: the sovereignty is lost through breach of faith, the kingdom is not. Ellicott marks the change of agent: until now all was done through a foreign king pursuing his own ends, and here God acts directly.

Whom the sprig means is barely disputed. Ellicott holds that the allegory requires a historical person and the description allows only one, as nearly all interpreters, Jewish and Christian, have read it, and notes that the word for tender bears on lowliness of origin, used elsewhere of a king describing his own weakness. Clarke expects a monarchy in the same line, a tender plant in its incarnation and eminent afterward; Wesley calls the eminence spiritual rather than splendid. Henry allows a partial fulfilment in the man who led the return.

Calvin resists collapsing the two. The prophets, he says, do not confine such promises to one person; they begin at the return from exile, the first instalment of the liberty afterwards made plain, and Christian writers who insist that all such language means Christ alone make themselves ridiculous to Jewish readers. His own frame is wider: the reign begins with the rebuilding of the temple after the seventy years and ends neither at the ascension nor in the early centuries but runs through that kingdom's whole progress to the last day.

The growth is the marvel. Calvin observes that cedars are slow, so a twig becoming a great tree quickly exceeds the ordinary rule of nature, and connects it with the older promise of a shoot from a stump, where the family is named for an obscure private man as though the king's memory were lost. Ellicott contrasts the goodly cedar with the low vine of the parable, and finds the same figure in a contemporary prophet and in a parable of Jesus.

The mountain and the birds go together. Gill reports the Jewish opinion that the land stood higher than all others and the city highest in it, where the preaching and the miracles happened and the first church was planted. Ellicott identifies it with Zion but warns against pressing the literal hill, taking it for the seat of the kingdom, and draws out the principle that the later dispensation is rooted in the earlier, the new covenant remaining a covenant with the old people. Clarke turns the tree into an inventory: boughs for apostles and successors, fruit for converts, birds of every wing for all nations, shade for trust that saves. Wesley says peace and safety.

The closing reversal divides them over the trees. Clarke reads four reigns — a high tree dethroned, a low one raised in his place, a green one dried when a father watched his sons killed, a dry one made to flourish in the promised heir — while reporting another commentator who takes high and green for the conqueror and low and dry for the conquered; Wesley makes the high tree the empire itself, brought down at last by its own conquerors. Ellicott and Calvin generalise, the other trees standing for every earthly power that must finally acknowledge the work. Ellicott sets the reversal beside the two songs celebrating the same overturning and calls it comfort for a Church in desolation. Calvin faces the contradiction between plucking a twig from a lofty cedar and raising what was low, and resolves it by the two states of one person, whose beginning was from eternity and who took the form of a slave.
